title: Base-Rate Neglect
hook: One vivid case can shove the usual numbers off the table.
coreIdea: Base-rate neglect happens when a specific story, symptom, or description crowds out what normally happens in the larger group.
counterintuition: The vivid case may matter, but it should not start from zero. First ask what usually happens, then let the case details move you from that starting point.
tryThisNow: Before your next judgment about a case, write the normal rate for the larger group, then add which details should move you up or down.
keyTakeaway: Start with what usually happens, then adjust.

breakdown.fastRead:
The parking ticket sits beside the hotel overbooking sheet while Ava listens to one guest's dramatic story. The story is sharp. The hotel still needs the base rate.

Base-rate neglect appears when a case description overwhelms the larger pattern. One angry guest, one strange symptom, one memorable accident, or one persuasive profile can make you forget how often the event normally happens.

The usual rate is the starting line.

The correction is to ask what happens in the relevant group first. Then use the case details to adjust, not to replace the base rate.
breakdown.deepRead:
The parking ticket on Ava's overbooking desk comes from a guest who arrived late, lost his room, and wrote a furious complaint. The night manager wants to stop overbooking on weekends. Ava can feel the pull of the case: tired guest, ruined anniversary, full parking lot, bad review.

The case matters. It should be read carefully. But it is not the whole population. Ava marks base rate risk on the parking ticket and asks for the last twelve months: how often weekend overbooking caused a walk, how often no-shows left empty rooms, and how often nearby hotels absorbed late arrivals. The single complaint becomes evidence inside a larger pattern.

A story needs a denominator.

Marc sees the same error in a chemicals plant incentive review. A safety glove sits beside a report about one operator who skipped a checklist after a bonus change. The case sounds like proof that the incentive is dangerous. Marc marks prior probability risk on the glove and asks how often checklist skips occurred before the bonus existed.

The base rate does not erase the case. It disciplines it. If the usual rate was low and now it is rising, the case may signal a real change. If the usual rate was already high, the vivid case may simply be the one people remember. Either way, the judgment improves when the case starts from the normal rate.

Begin with the population, then move.
breakdown.fullRead:
The pediatric clinic smells of disinfectant and crayons while Sienna studies a ticket stub from a crowded appointment desk. A parent describes a rare diagnosis she found online, and the symptoms partly fit. The story is vivid because it is about one child in front of the room. The ordinary diagnosis is less dramatic because it belongs to thousands of children.

Base-rate neglect is not a failure to care about the case. It is a failure to anchor the case in the right group. Symptoms, profiles, customer stories, interview impressions, and risk reports all arrive with detail. Detail makes them feel specific, and specific can feel more accurate than general. But prediction starts with the broader pattern: what usually happens among children with these symptoms, guests with this booking pattern, farms under this weather setup, or drivers at this rental counter?

Work on the psychology of prediction made this conflict famous: people often let a rich case description overpower base rates. The old medical warning about hoofbeats points in the same direction. If common causes are common and rare causes are rare, the first move is not to chase the most striking match. The first move is to know the usual rate.

What is the base rate before the story begins?

Sienna writes that question on the ticket stub. Then she separates the work. The parent's details go in one column. The clinic's frequency data goes in another: common diagnoses for age, season, exposure, and symptom cluster. The rare diagnosis is not mocked or ignored. It is weighted after the ordinary rates are visible.

You can feel this in a farm rainfall projection. You are holding a thermometer in Tobias's equipment shed after one field looks exactly like last year's drought pattern. The case description is tempting: same heat, same cracked topsoil, same anxious call from the irrigation supplier. Tobias must decide whether to order emergency water based on that resemblance or start with the base rate for rainfall after this weather setup.

Base rates keep resemblance from becoming prophecy.

A car-rental desk creates the same pressure in miniature. Jade hears a vivid story about a tourist who declined insurance and paid for a scratched bumper. The price card suddenly looks cheap. But before buying the upsell, she needs the usual rate of damage for that route, car class, and rental length. The story may move the estimate. It should not become the estimate.

Start with what usually happens, then adjust.
breakdown.whyItMatters: Base-rate neglect makes the memorable case feel more informative than the broader pattern. Readers need to anchor judgments in normal frequencies before case detail changes the estimate.

reviewCards.front: A case story is vivid. What should you ask before judging it?
reviewCards.back: Ask what usually happens in the relevant larger group.

reviewCards.front: Why can a detailed profile mislead prediction?
reviewCards.back: Detail can feel more diagnostic than it is and crowd out the base rate.

reviewCards.front: How should a rare diagnosis be handled?
reviewCards.back: Keep it in view, but start with common rates for the symptom cluster and adjust from there.

reviewCards.front: What makes a case detail useful?
reviewCards.back: It should have proven predictive value that justifies moving the estimate away from the base rate.

reviewCards.front: What is the core base-rate correction?

implementationPlan.coreSkill: You learn to anchor judgments in normal rates before case detail moves the estimate.

ifThenPlans.plan: If one complaint drives a policy debate, then I will ask for the full rate across comparable cases.
If a rare explanation fits a case, then I will first list the common explanations for the same symptom cluster.
If a case resembles a past event, then I will check how often similar cases actually led to that outcome.
If someone matches a memorable profile, then I will ask how often that profile predicts success.
